how-to-bid-a-fence-job.html.text:
FENCE CONTRACTORS

How to bid a fence job without a flat price per foot

Homeowners google “fence installation cost per foot” and call you with a number they found on a forum. If you match it, you have quoted their yard as if it were a roll of fencing. It is not. After using the fence bid calculator, you can send a price that already counted the posts, the gates, and the tear-out — work that used to hide inside a scratch-pad per-foot guess.

Count the posts first

A run of L feet on spacing S needs a post at each end plus one every S feet: ceil(L ÷ S) + 1. A 140-foot backyard on 8-foot centers is 19 posts, not 140 ÷ 8 = 17.5 rounded however feels lucky. Each corner adds a terminal that is not already on that straight spacing.

Ends, corners, and gate posts are terminals — heavier stock, more concrete, more time. Line posts are cheaper. If you price every post as a line post, the hardware invoice is already over the bid.

Gates are not fence

A 4-foot walk gate and a 12-foot drive gate remove 16 feet of infill and add two kits plus hang time. Treating those 16 feet as privacy panels understates material and understates labor. The calculator subtracts the openings from infill and prices the kits and hours separately.

Tear-out and dirt are hours, not footage

Pulling 40 feet of rotten stockade does not add 40 feet you can bill at the new-fence rate. It adds haul, dump, and crew time. Clay and rock do not change the panel price; they change how long each hole takes. Multiply labor hours by the site, not the material.

Build the number the same way every time

  1. Split the job into runs (front vs back, wood vs chain-link).
  2. Count posts from spacing, then upgrade terminals for ends, corners, and gates.
  3. Price infill, posts, gates, concrete, and tear-out from your last invoices.
  4. Load the wage with payroll burden. Add permits, dump, and travel.
  5. Recover overhead as a percent of that direct cost. Set margin as a share of the price, not a markup on cost.
  6. Read the walk-away number — total cost — before you answer “can you do it for $35 a foot?”

A number that looks cheap is usually underwater

On a typical 140-foot, 6-foot wood privacy run with two corners, one walk gate, one drive gate, 40 feet of tear-out, and heavy clay, a $35/ft Facebook quote is below cost once posts and gates are counted. The installed price per foot on that job is a result, not an input. Quote the job, then glance at the per-foot figure to see whether you are in the range the homeowner has heard — and whether matching it would lose money.

Open the calculator and replace the starting figures with your own. Nothing is uploaded.

Common questions

How do you calculate how many fence posts you need?

Posts along a run equal ceil(linear feet ÷ post spacing) + 1, plus one extra terminal for each corner. A 140-foot run on 8-foot centers is 19 posts; two corners make 21. Ends, corners, and gate posts are terminals and cost more than line posts.

Why is a flat fence price per foot often wrong?

A flat installed price assumes every foot is the same. Gates replace infill but add hardware and hang time. Corners and ends need heavier terminals and more concrete. Tear-out and rocky digging add hours with no extra footage to bill. Two 140-foot jobs can differ by thousands of dollars.

What should a fence bid include besides material?

Loaded labor (wage plus payroll burden), concrete, gate hardware, tear-out and haul, permits and travel, overhead, and a target margin as a share of the price — not a markup on cost. The walk-away number is total cost, below which the job makes nothing.

No warranty. This page is not legal, tax, financial, engineering, or business advice, and it does not tell you what to charge. Verify every figure against your own costs and a qualified professional before submitting a bid.

FOR FENCE CONTRACTORS

Bid the posts and the gates, not the linear feet.

Price a fence install the way the job actually costs: posts from your spacing, heavier terminals at ends, corners, and gates, tear-out, and the extra hours clay or rock will eat. You get the job price, what it works out to per foot and per labor hour, and the number below which the job loses money.

The fence

One row per run — front vs back, or wood vs chain-link. Pick a material to start from common figures, then replace every cost and hour with numbers from your last invoice and your last timed job.

Site and tear-out

Your costs

Payroll burden covers employer taxes, workers’ compensation, liability insurance, and paid time off. Underestimating it — or bidding rocky dirt at a flat per-foot number — is the usual reason a fence job that looked profitable was not.

Hand the customer a proposal

The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

Where the money goes

    Common questions

    What does this fence estimate include?

    Each run’s material and posts by length and post spacing, with extra terminal posts at corners and gates, gate material and labor, concrete per post, tear-out of an existing fence, harder digging or a sloped yard, and overhead and margin on top.

    How does difficult digging or a sloped yard change the price?

    Rocky or clay soil and a mild or steep slope multiply the labor hours on posts and tear-out. Concrete and panels cost the same regardless of ground condition, so only the crew-time estimate changes, not the material pricing.

    Why do gates change the post count, not just add a gate price?

    A line post next to a gate has to become a heavier terminal post to carry the hinge or latch, and a short run mostly taken up by a gate may need an extra terminal altogether. The calculator upgrades and adds posts automatically so the total reflects that instead of undercounting them.

    Does the tool know local frost depth, property lines, or permit requirements?

    No. Post spacing, concrete per post, and any permit-adjacent cost are numbers you supply yourself, and there is no frost-depth table, property-line check, or permit lookup built in. Confirm those with your local building department and a survey before you dig.

    Is my data uploaded anywhere?

    No account and no network requests — everything runs in your browser. The only thing saved between visits is your business and contact details for the printed proposal, and you can clear those with “Forget my business details.”

    What’s the difference between the total cost and the price shown?

    Total cost is materials, posts, gates, tear-out, and labor plus overhead — the walk-away number. The price shown applies your target margin on top, so it is what you’d charge to hit that margin rather than just cover your costs.

vs-a-flat-price-per-foot.html.text:
← Fence Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat price-per-foot quote

"$35 a foot installed" is not a price for a fence — it is a price for one flat run with no gates, quietly applied to a corner-heavy yard with tear-out and hard digging.

What a flat price-per-foot quote is

A flat per-foot number is the fastest way to bid over the phone or match a homeowner's forum post: one figure, easy to multiply by any run length, and the number a caller holding a competitor's estimate will ask you to match on their own yard.

The number behind it was set for one job — usually a flat, easy run with no corners, no gates, normal soil, and nothing to tear out — and then reused for every fence afterward, whether or not the next yard has terminals at every corner, a walk gate and a drive gate, an old fence to pull, or clay that slows every post hole.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter each run's length, post spacing, corners, and gates, the existing fence to tear out, the digging condition and slope, and your own material and labor rates. It prices posts, terminals, gates, tear-out, and the extra hours harder digging adds separately, and returns a walk-away price and price per foot below which the job loses money — for this yard, not a generic one.

Job$35/ft quoteWalk-away priceVerdict
140 ft chain-link, 4 ft, no corners, no gates, normal soil, no tear-out$4,900.00$2,532.76Covers, $2,367.24 to spare
140 ft wood privacy, 6 ft, 2 corners, walk + drive gate, heavy clay, 40 ft tear-out (this calculator's own default job)$4,900.00$6,033.93Short $1,133.93
220 ft vinyl privacy, 6 ft, 3 corners, walk + drive gate, rocky/steep, 60 ft tear-out$7,700.00$16,261.98Short $8,561.98

Worked using this calculator's own material presets at a $25 hourly wage, 28% payroll burden, 15% overhead on direct cost, and a 25% target margin — the form's own shipped defaults, not numbers invented for this page. Open the calculator to check any row yourself.

Notice the middle row: it is this calculator's own shipped starting point, not a job picked to prove a point, and a $35/ft quote already falls over a thousand dollars short of it. One old fence to tear out, one more corner, or one gate is the difference between a flat rate that happens to work and one that does not.

What a flat price-per-foot quote doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same rate whether the run is a flat chain-link stretch with no gates or a corner-heavy privacy fence — counting terminal posts the same as cheaper line posts either way. Counts posts from run length and spacing, then upgrades ends, corners, and gate posts to heavier terminals, so a corner-heavy yard prices differently from a flat run.
Has no separate line for a walk gate or a drive gate, so hardware and hang time are absorbed into the same per-foot number as plain infill. Subtracts gate openings from infill and prices gate material and hang hours per gate, scaled to walk or drive width.
Prices "a fence" the same whether or not an old one has to come out first. Adds tear-out hours and haul cost per foot only when there is an existing fence to pull.
Has no line for clay, rock, or a sloped yard, so a hard dig gets the same price as a flat, easy one. Multiplies labor hours by a dig-condition and slope multiplier entered for the actual site.
Gives the homeowner a price to shop, not a number to check a quote against when their yard turns out to have three corners and 40 feet of rotten fence to remove after the flat rate was already promised. Reports the walk-away price and price per foot for the job as entered, so a shopped rate can be scored against real cost before it is confirmed.

A flat price-per-foot quote is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied to a run, corner count, gate set, or digging condition it was not set on, and "a fence" alone never tells you that has happened. This calculator does not replace judgment about your market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat rate skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat price-per-foot fence quote get the price wrong?

Because fence cost scales with posts, terminals, gates, tear-out, and digging conditions — not with linear feet alone. A flat run of chain-link with no gates and easy digging is a different job from the same footage in 6-foot wood privacy with two corners, a walk gate, a drive gate, tear-out of the old fence, and heavy clay. A flat per-foot price quotes both the same and is wrong on one of them every time.

What does a flat price-per-foot quote usually leave out entirely?

Terminal posts at corners and gates, gate material and hang time, tear-out of an existing fence, and the extra labor hours that clay, rock, or a slope add to every hole. A published per-foot number is set on one configuration — usually a flat, easy run with no gates and normal soil — and has no separate line for any of those.

How much do corners, gates, and tear-out actually add over a flat rate?

On this calculator's own worked examples, at a $25 hourly wage, 28% burden, 15% overhead, and a 25% target margin: 140 feet of chain-link with no corners, no gates, and no tear-out walks away at $2,532.76, comfortably under a $35/ft, $4,900.00 quote. This calculator's own shipped default job — 140 feet of 6-foot wood privacy with two corners, a walk gate, a drive gate, and 40 feet of tear-out in heavy clay — walks away at $6,033.93, $1,133.93 short of that same $35/ft number. A 220-foot vinyl-privacy run with three corners, two gates, 60 feet of tear-out, rocky digging, and a steep slope walks away at $16,261.98, $8,561.98 short of a $35/ft, $7,700.00 quote.

Is a flat price-per-foot quote ever the right way to bid a fence?

For something close to the easy run it was probably priced on — flat ground, no corners, no gates, nothing to tear out — a flat rate can land close, and on this calculator's own numbers that easy job clears a $35/ft quote with over $2,100 to spare. The risk is corners, gates, tear-out, and hard digging stacking on top of each other, because a flat per-foot price has no way to see any of them until the crew is already on site.

Does this calculator know what to charge in my market?

No. It has no data on local material costs or what competitors charge. It takes the runs, posts, gates, tear-out, and digging conditions you enter, plus your own wage, burden, and overhead, and turns them into a walk-away price for the job you describe — the arithmetic a flat per-foot number skips, not a market survey.

Nothing here says or implies that quoting a flat price-per-foot is a bad-faith practice — it is a common, honest shortcut that works until the job stops matching the run, gates, and ground it was set on. This page describes where that shortcut breaks down, not a fault in anyone who uses it.

vs-fence-cloud.html.text:
← Fence Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. Fence Cloud

Two different shapes: Fence Cloud is an account-based CRM and estimating platform for running a fence company's whole lead-to-job pipeline. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this one fence install cost, given its posts, gates, and tear-out, before you send the bid.

What each tool is for

Fence Cloud is a cloud-based CRM and estimating platform built specifically for fence contractors. It covers lead and project tracking with contact management, activity logs, and advanced search; material-breakdown estimating across chain link, wood, vinyl, ornamental, and agricultural/split-rail fence, including mixing suppliers or materials and marking up drawings; and auto-filled, customizable paperwork — contracts, packing lists, labor worksheets, gate cut sheets, work orders, and foreman reports — meant to take a job from lead through completion inside one account. It is sold as an ongoing subscription. Fence Cloud's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — fence-specific CRM plus estimating, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for Fence Cloud appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what Fence Cloud does. It does not track a lead, generate a cut sheet, or hold a record across jobs. It takes one fence install — posts counted from run length and spacing, heavier terminals at ends, corners, and gates, panel infill after gate openings come out, tear-out, and clay, rock, or slope conditions — plus loaded labor, other direct cost, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into the job price, the price per linear foot, the effective hourly rate, the post and gate counts, the material split, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money, plus a copyable plain-text bid summary. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I run a fence company and need leads, estimates, and job paperwork tracked in one system across every crew and every job.Fence Cloud, or a comparable fence-specific CRM — running the whole pipeline is not something this calculator does.
Does the price for this one fence job actually clear my cost and target margin, once posts, terminals, gates, and tear-out are counted correctly?This calculator — free, instant, private, no account.
How many posts does a run actually need once corners and gates upgrade some of them to terminals?This calculator's own post-and-terminal count from your spacing.
I need my whole sales and install team working the same leads and paperwork from one shared account.Fence Cloud — built as an ongoing, account-based platform for exactly that job.
How does the math behind a per-job fence price actually work?This calculator's own bidding walkthrough.
Do I need to create an account or sign up to use the tool?This calculator: no. Fence Cloud is used through a subscription account.

Most fence contractors get different value from each: Fence Cloud (or a comparable platform) for running the company's whole lead-to-job pipeline and paperwork as an ongoing account, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login check on whether one job's price actually clears cost and margin before the bid goes out. This page's own figures are a pricing model, not a lead record, a cut sheet, or a signed contract.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or Fence Cloud?

They do different jobs. Fence Cloud is a cloud-based CRM and estimating platform built specifically for fence contractors, covering lead and project tracking, material-breakdown estimates across chain link, wood, vinyl, ornamental, and agricultural/split-rail fence, and auto-filled paperwork such as contracts, packing lists, labor worksheets, gate cut sheets, work orders, and foreman reports. It is sold as an ongoing subscription account for running a fence company's whole lead-to-job pipeline. This calculator does none of that. It takes one fence install — posts from run length and spacing, heavier terminals at ends, corners, and gates, tear-out, and digging conditions — and turns that into the job price, price per linear foot, effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money, plus a copyable bid summary, instantly, in the browser, with no account and nothing uploaded. A fence company running leads and paperwork across every job at once is better served by Fence Cloud or a comparable platform; a contractor who wants an instant, private, correctly-sized price for one job before a bid goes out is in the right place here.
